Most shared iSNVs remained at low frequency and did not correspond to fixed differences among the MV Hondius outbreak genomes, consistent with limited diversification during the observed transmission chain. However, several within-host variable positions also overlapped sites reconstructed as substitutions along the outbreak-lineage ancestral branches of one or more of the five human outbreaks, including S: C1116T; L:A704G, L:T3560C, L: T6302C, and M:G1164A (see Supplementary Tables 7 and 8). Together, these findings show that the MV Hondius outbreak contained greater low-frequency diversity than was visible from consensus genomes, while providing no evidence that a new variant rose to fixation during the sampled outbreak.

Discussion

The central implication of our analysis is that recent human Andes virus outbreaks are consistent with independent emergences from long-standing, geographically structured reservoir diversity, rather than as a single recently emerged human-transmissible lineage or a repeated, obvious adaptive transition immediately before detection. Across five recorded human outbreak lineages, viruses involved in person-to-person transmission were embedded within broader ANDV diversity sampled from humans and rodents and arose in distinct phylogenetic and regional backgrounds. Our analyses place these observations in a comprehensive segment-linked dataset and a common cross-segment molecular dating framework that retains incompletely sampled isolates. The available genomes suggest that multiple reservoir-associated lineages may already possess some capacity to generate limited human transmission chains. Isolated human infections interspersed among rodent-derived and outbreak-associated diversity further argue against a simple dichotomy between intrinsically non-transmissible reservoir viruses and recently adapted human-transmissible lineages.

Our analysis also addresses a broader methodological challenge in the evolutionary study of segmented viruses. Historical datasets frequently contain incomplete segment sets, inconsistent accession linkage, and different taxon compositions among segment alignments. Restricting analyses to observed segment sequences can discard known relationships among sampled viruses and destabilise inference in sparsely represented segments. Our linkage-informed representation retained real sampled taxa without imputing nucleotide states and allowed isolate identity, sampling time, and segmentsupported phylogenetic placement to be represented more consistently across segmentspecific time trees. This was particularly valuable for the L segment, where it stabilised inference and recovered temporal model support in a dataset that was unstable using observed sequences alone. It also improved cross-segment comparability for the Chile 2024 lineage: because its closest comparator lacked an observed L segment, the observed-only analysis produced a substantially older time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA), whereas linkage-informed representation brought the L-segment estimate into much closer agreement with S and M. The approach is intentionally conservative because it does not account for uncertainty in the constrained topology or reconstruct missing nucleotide states and therefore cannot establish whether an unobserved segment was reassorted. Its benefit should therefore be interpreted as improved use of known linkage and sampling information rather than automatically more accurate reconstruction. Used alongside observed-sequence-only analyses, this framework provides a general way to quantify how patchy segment coverage affects molecular dating inference, particularly by assessing its impact on the compatibility of tMRCA estimates across segments.

Our molecular clock analyses indicate that the evolutionary history of ANDV extends substantially beyond the recent human outbreaks through which many lineages were first recognised. Across nested datasets, the more phylogenetically restricted clades generally produced higher substitution rate estimates, whereas inclusion of progressively older reservoir-associated diversity lowered inferred rates, consistent with timedependent rate variation and strong purifying selection. Our PoW estimates were older than corresponding tip-dated estimates, with broadly overlapping 95% HPDs for the observed and linkage-informed clades 1-4 datasets, but substantially deeper estimates after inclusion of unclassified diversity. The strongest signal came from the M segment, which contained the greatest number of observed divergent unclassified sequences and placed the sampled root at approximately 17,000 years before present, whereas corresponding S-and L-segment estimates were more uncertain because several unclassified taxa were represented by linkage-informed missing-segment entries. Similar discrepancies between recent tip-dated estimates and deeper evolutionary histories have been reported for Puumala and Tula hantaviruses 22 . Together, these results caution against extrapolating short-term evolutionary rates across deep hantavirus timescales and suggest that the lineages underlying recent ANDV outbreaks may have evolved over much longer periods than their recent detection implies. This distinction matters for how ANDV emergence is interpreted. The observation of person-to-person spread naturally raises concern that a lineage has acquired new mutations increasing transmissibility in humans. However, our analyses provide little support for a repeated, recent adaptive transition. Branches leading to human outbreaks were dominated by synonymous change, relaxed clock analyses did not identify consistent acceleration on outbreak lineage ancestral branches, branch-specific selection analyses did not detect reproducible evidence of episodic diversifying selection, and structural mapping did not point to any recurrent changes in antigenic, entry, fusion, or polymerase active-site regions. Although several lineage-specific amino acid changes occurred in the glycoprotein or polymerase and remain plausible candidates for experimental follow-up, they affected different sites and structural environments, were generally conservative, and did not converge on a shared functional mechanism. We therefore interpret these substitutions as candidate lineage-specific changes rather than evidence of a common adaptive transition.

An alternative hypothesis is that the capacity for limited human-to-human transmission is an existing property of parts of ANDV diversity, rather than a newly acquired feature of each outbreak lineage. This would imply that outbreaks occur when a reservoir lineage with permissive viral properties enters a favourable ecological and epidemiological context: close contact, delayed diagnosis, household or healthcare transmission, or host factors that allow unusually successful infection 9 . The fact that multiple phylogenetically distinct lineages have caused isolated human infections or limited transmission clusters, yet none has established sustained circulation in humans, is consistent with this interpretation. If a single recent mutation were sufficient to create a stably humantransmissible virus, repeated emergence might be expected to produce more consistent genomic signatures or more persistent transmission. Instead, the key determinant of outbreak risk may lie as much in repeated opportunities for old reservoir lineages to enter settings where limited human transmission becomes possible as in recent adaptive genetic changes in the virus. Limited transmission is therefore likely to reflect an interaction between pre-existing viral properties and contingent ecological, epidemiological, and host conditions.

We also saw limited diversity within the current MV Hondius 2026 outbreak. Across the three genomes analysed here, including paired blood and nasal samples from the same individual, we observed only a single consensus-level difference: the synonymous Lsegment mutation L:C2144T. This is also consistent with an independent raw-read-based analysis of additional outbreak sequences, which reported only one further L-segment mutation among samples not included in this study 21 . Our within-host analysis nevertheless identified additional low-frequency variation shared between paired blood and nasal samples, including nonsynonymous variants in the nucleocapsid protein and polymerase. Several variable positions also overlapped sites reconstructed as substitutions along outbreak-lineage ancestral branches. This recurrence across within-host and phylogenetic timescales does not establish adaptation, but it identifies a small set of sites that may be mutationally accessible, selectively tolerated, or functionally relevant. Importantly, none of these variants showed evidence of rising to fixation during the sampled outbreak, supporting the broader conclusion that the MV Hondius transmission chain was not accompanied by an obvious recent adaptive sweep.

Our results also refine what should be tested experimentally. Rather than asking only whether each recent outbreak lineage recently acquired a single transmission-enhancing mutation, future work should ask whether different ANDV clades vary in baseline phenotypes relevant to spillover and person-to-person spread. These include glycoprotein-mediated entry, particle stability, replication efficiency, innate immune antagonism, tissue tropism, shedding, and environmental persistence. The candidate mutations identified here provide a focused starting point, but the broader hypothesis is that phenotypic differences among ANDV lineages may have accumulated deeper in reservoir evolution, before the recent human outbreaks sampled to date.

The geographic patterning of the closest sampled relatives also has direct implications for surveillance. The MV Hondius 2026 lineage is linked to a cross-border southern Chilenorthern Patagonia assemblage, the Epuyén and Argentina 2014 lineages to Río Negroand Chubut-associated diversity, and the Chile 2024 lineage to Neuquén-associated diversity. These patterns are consistent with strong geographic structure within ANDV, but we note that exact phylogeographic reconstruction of the closest ancestor remains challenging given sparse reservoir sampling and incomplete segment sequencing which can dominate uncertainty in timing and immediate ancestry of each outbreak. Surveillance should therefore not focus only on descendants of previously recognised outbreak viruses, because the relevant risk appears to be distributed across incompletely sampled regional reservoir diversity. In summary, our results suggest that recent human ANDV outbreaks are not the product of obvious, repeated adaptive bursts immediately before detection, but rather sporadic emergences from old, structured, and incompletely sampled reservoir lineages. By integrating new MV Hondius sequence data with a comprehensive segment-linked collection that retains partial and incomplete genomes, the study provides both a broader empirical reconstruction of ANDV diversity and a linkage-informed missing-segment framework for molecular dating of patchy segmented datasets. Systematic temporalsignal testing, time-dependent rate analysis, and PoW modelling place recent outbreaks against a much deeper reservoir-associated history, while substitution reconstruction, selection analysis, branch-rate estimation, structural mapping, and within-host analysis identify no common recent adaptive transition preceding person-to-person transmission. This shifts the question from whether each outbreak lineage newly adapted to humans to which lineage-level phenotypes evolved during deeper ANDV history and which ecological, epidemiological, and host conditions occasionally permit human transmission without sustained circulation.

Methods

Sequence generation and consensus calling

Two primary genome sequences from the current MV Hondius-associated Andes virus outbreak were generated from paired clinical samples collected from the same individual on the same day: a whole-blood sample (XDHK) and a nasopharyngeal swab sample (XDJH). Laboratory processing followed the tiled-amplification approach described previously for Andes virus sequencing 23 https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/Q8Qs using Oxford Nanopore MinION sequencing.

Viral RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA kit (Qiagen). Reverse transcription was performed using SuperScript IV reverse transcriptase (ThermoFisher Scientific), following the manufacturer's recommendations, with 8 μl of extracted RNA as input. PCR amplification was carried out using Phusion U Multiplex Master Mix (ThermoFisher Scientific), with 2 μl of cDNA template in 25 μl reactions. Cycling conditions were 98°C for 2 min, followed by 45 cycles of 98°C for 30 s and 65°C for 5 min, with a final extension at 72°C for 10 min.

PCR products were purified using 0.8× MagMAX PureBind magnetic beads (ThermoFisher Scientific), washed twice with 80% ethanol, and eluted in 20 μl of 1 mM Tris pH 8.0. Purified amplicon pools were quantified using the Qubit Broad Range dsDNA 1× assay kit (ThermoFisher Scientific) and combined in equal proportions where possible. Pooled amplicons were prepared for sequencing using the Native Barcoding Kit V14 (SQK-NBD114.24; Oxford Nanopore Technologies) and sequenced on a MinION Mk1D device using a FLO-MIN114 flow cell.

Raw sequence data were analysed using nf-ViralMutations (https://github.com/phac-nml/nf-ViralMutations; commit 8675768). Reads were aligned to Andes virus reference sequences and processed to generate segment-specific consensus sequences and base-frequency summaries. Human and other off-target reads were removed before downstream analysis. Consensus positions were masked when read support was below 20. In the event that two or more mutations combine to more than 70% (e.g. one mutation at 35% and one at 40%), then the IUPAC ambiguous base of the mutations is called.

Sequence and corresponding data curation

We downloaded all nucleotide sequences classified in the species Orthohantavirus andesense (taxid: 1980456) available on the NCBI Virus database as of the 26 th of May 2026. Additionally, we included the first genome of the recent MV Hondius 2026 outbreak sampled in Switzerland (Pathoplexus: PP_006WBLH.2, GenBank: L -PZ385161.1, M -PZ385162.1, S -PZ385163.1, ANDV/Switzerland/Hu-3337/2026) as well as two sequences from the same patient of the outbreak generated as part of this study (Pathoplexus: PP_006XDJH.5 and PP_006XDHK.5). Lastly, the reference genome of Sin Nombre virus (GenBank: L -NC_077671.1, M -NC_077670.1, S -NC_077669.1) was included in the analysis as an outgroup. Metadata were harmonised across sources, including accession, segment, host, country, region or province where available, collection date, source study, and data-use status. Sequences were excluded from downstream analysis if they were derived from experimental passage (Supplementary Table 1). For records without exact collection dates, we consulted the source publications and assigned bounded sampling intervals. These intervals were incorporated as uniform tip-date priors in BEAST analyses (Supplementary Table 3, Supplementary Figure 6 7 8).

Multiple sequence alignment

Before constructing the sequence alignments, partial M segment sequences covering different parts of the same virus genome segment (Gc/Gn) were manually concatenated based on their isolate names and information available in their original publication. Nucleotide sequences of each segment were then aligned using mafft v7.505 --localpair option 24 . These alignments were manually trimmed to their coding sequences and translated using BioEdit 25 and realigned on the amino acid level with mafft --localpair. The resulting amino acid alignments were converted to their corresponding codon alignments using pal2nal v14 26 https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/7cOe which were used for all phylogenetic and selection analysis described below. Coding-region coordinates were defined relative to the Andes virus reference genome https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/C67E as follows: S segment, nucleotides 43-1329; M segment, nucleotides 52-3468; and L segment, nucleotides 36-6497.

Maximum-likelihood phylogenetics and clade definition

Maximum-likelihood trees were inferred separately for the S, M and L segment codon alignments using IQ-TREE v2.3.https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/kdox 27 . ModelFinderPlus was used to identify best-fitting nucleotide substitution models 28 https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/oLeG and branch support was assessed with 10,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates 29 . The species tree was separated into ANDV-like background and ANDV, focusing on the four ANDV clades defined consistent with Bellomo et al 6 . Sequences within ANDV diversity that were not monophyletic with any of the four clades were annotated as "unclassified" (Supplementary Figures 1 2 3). Trees were visualised and annotated in FigTree (https://github.com/rambaut/figtree).

For each outbreak-associated lineage, we compared the reconstructed sequence at the closest sampled common ancestor with the reconstructed sequence on the branch leading to the outbreak cluster. Nucleotide changes were annotated by segment, genomic coordinate, codon, codon position, and amino acid change using custom R script.

Reconstruction of linked genome-segment datasets

ANDV sequence records were linked across the S, M, and L genome segments using isolate names, accession metadata, source publications, sampling location, host, and collection date. Segment linkages were accepted only where the records could be assigned to the same sampled virus with high confidence. The resulting linkage table is provided in Supplementary Table 2.

For a sampled virus with an observed sequence for at least one genome segment but no available sequence for another segment(s), we created a linkage-informed missingsegment entry. This entry consisted entirely of N characters and matched the length of the corresponding segment alignment. It was assigned the same isolate identifier, host metadata, and sampling date as the linked observed segment. No nucleotide state was imputed.

The placement of each missing-segment taxon was constrained to the clade supported by its observed linked segment, while relationships within that clade remained estimated from the segment-specific data. This approach assumes that the missing segment has not undergone reassortment that would place it outside the clade supported by the observed linked segment. Although this assumption cannot be tested directly for an unsequenced segment, reassortment was limited across the sampled ANDV phylogenies and was not detected among the outbreak lineages or their closest comparator sequences (i.e., non-outbreak sequences that provide phylogenetic context for placing and dating outbreak lineages within broader ANDV diversity). We therefore considered clade-level placement to be a reasonable working assumption, while retaining observedsequence-only analyses as sensitivity analyses.

Because all-N sequences are uninformative with respect to nucleotide character likelihood, these entries contributed no direct sequence evidence. Their purpose was to preserve known taxon linkage, sampling time, and topological representation across segment-specific analyses.

Molecular clock analyses

Time-scaled phylogenies were inferred using BEAST 2 v2.6.https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/Niku 30 . Analyses were performed separately for each genome segment and for pre-defined outbreak-associated clade subsets containing human outbreak lineages and their nearest available human-or rodent-derived comparator sequences.

For the primary dated analyses, we focused on ANDV clades 1-4 and five outbreaks with documented person-to-person transmission where sequence data were available: MV Hondius 2026, Chile 2011, Argentina 2014, Epuyén 2018/19, and Chile 2024. M-segment data were available for all five, whereas S and L analyses included four because comparable sequence data were unavailable for Chile 2024. EU241684.1 (S) and EU241643.1-EU241657.1 (M) had discordant or weakly supported placements between maximum-likelihood and BEAST trees. In the BEAST time trees, these sequences fell outside clades 1-4 and were treated as unclassified in downstream analyses.

Primary analyses used a strict molecular clock and constant size coalescent prior. Complementary uncorrelated lognormal relaxed clock analyses were performed for S, M, and L to compare branch-specific rates across the full clades 1-4 dataset, the MV Hondius-related clades 1+3 subset, and the Epuyén-related clade 2 subset (Supplementary Tables 4 and 5). Strict clock analyses converged consistently and were used for the main node-date estimates. Relaxed clock analyses were used for branchrate comparisons and sensitivity analyses rather than for the primary dates.

Analyses used an HKY substitution model. Uniform priors ranging from 10 -12 to 10 -2 substitutions/site/year were assigned to strict clock rate and relaxed clock mean parameters. MCMC chains were run for 10-400 million iterations, with the first 10% discarded as burn-in. Convergence and mixing were assessed using Tracer v1.7.https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/7vs5 31 https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/7vs5 requiring effective sample size values above 200 for all the parameters included in the model. Maximum clade credibility (MCC) trees with median heights and assuming burnin of 10% were summarised using TreeAnnotator and visualised using FigTree v1.4.4.

Closest sampled common ancestors and outbreak-cluster sensitivity analyses

For each outbreak-associated lineage, we identified the posterior node corresponding to the closest sampled common ancestor between the outbreak lineage and its nearest available comparator sequence or comparator clade. Posterior distributions of these node dates were extracted from BEAST posterior trees. These dates were interpreted as closest sampled common ancestor dates, not as direct estimates of spillover timing or the first human infection.

Because several outbreak datasets contained multiple near-identical sequences from the same human transmission cluster, we performed sensitivity analyses to test whether dense outbreak sampling affected coalescent-based node-date estimates. For each outbreak cluster, we repeated primary analyses using a reduced dataset retaining two representative sequences per outbreak where available. Representative sequences were chosen to preserve temporal and genetic diversity within each outbreak while reducing overrepresentation of nearly identical genomes. These analyses were compared with the all-sequence analyses to assess whether inferred closest sampled common ancestor dates were robust to dense sampling of recent outbreak sequences. In parallel, we compared these datasets with the inclusion of linkage-informed missing-segment taxa to assess the effect of incomplete comparator-segment representation on divergence time and rate estimates.

Bayesian evaluation of temporal signal

Temporal signal was evaluated using Bayesian Evaluation of Temporal Signal (BETS) 12 . For each segment, heterochronous models incorporating observed sampling dates were compared with otherwise equivalent isochronous models in which all tips shared the same date. Analyses were conducted separately for clade 2, clades 1+3, clades 1-3, and clades 1-4. To assess sensitivity to initial topology, analyses were repeated with and without a starting tree where indicated. We separately ran the same set of tests for datasets containing linkage-informed missing-segment taxa only where observed-only datasets lacked support for temporal signal, for eg. L clade 1-3. For the S segment there were 12 missing samples, 6 for M, and 29 for L segment.

The heterochronous and isochronous models used identical substitution, molecular clock, and tree-prior specifications apart from their treatment of sampling times. Marginal likelihoods were estimated using stepping-stone sampling with 20 path steps, a chain length of 200 million per step, and 10% burn-in unless stated otherwise. Log Bayes factors were calculated as the difference between the log marginal likelihood of the heterochronous and isochronous models. Positive values favoured temporal structure, with values above +5 units interpreted as evidence for presence of temporal signal (see Supplementary Table 4).

Codon-based selection analyses

Selection analyses were performed across local outbreak-associated clades and broader ANDV phylogeny. We estimated site-specific and branch-specific dN/dS and used codonsubstitution methods 32 to test for pervasive negative selection (FEL) 33 https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/cRvW episodic diversifying selection (MEME and FEL) 34 and branch-specific shifts in selective pressure (aBSREL 35 https://paperpile.com/c/karsrEBu/ohg0 RELAX 36 ). Outbreak stem branches were labelled a priori to test whether they showed evidence of elevated nonsynonymous evolution relative to background branches.

Structural mapping of nonsynonymous mutations

Nonsynonymous mutations were mapped to available ANDV or homologous hantavirus protein structures. For the M-segment glycoprotein precursor, residues were interpreted relative to the deposited ANDV glycoprotein structure PDB 9P3I and published domain annotations for the Gn cytoplasmic tail, transmembrane region and putative RNP/Nprotein-binding region. For the L-segment RdRp mutation, no ANDV RdRp structure was available, so the mutation was mapped by sequence alignment to Hantaan virus RdRp structures, including the full-length RdRp structure PDB 8P1L and the endonucleasedomain structure PDB 5IZE. Structural context was assessed by residue location, solvent exposure, proximity to annotated functional regions, active sites, transmembrane regions, and unresolved loops and linkers.

Reconstruction of deeper evolutionary history of ANDV

To reconstruct deeper evolutionary timescales, we applied the Prisoner of War (PoW) model to broader ANDV diversity 8 . The PoW model maps ultrametric genetic-distance trees to time-scaled divergence trees by accounting for the decline in apparent substitution rate over longer evolutionary timescales. This approach is useful when shortterm rates estimated from measurably evolving datasets cannot be extrapolated linearly over deeper divergence times because of time-dependent rate variation.

We used posterior substitution rate distributions from the clade 2 dataset shown in Figure 2A as the short-term calibration for PoW reconstruction. For each segment, we then generated ultrametric genetic-distance trees for three datasets: ANDV clades 1-4, ANDV clades 1-4 including unclassified sequences, and ANDV clades 1-4 datasets containing linkage-informed missing-segment taxa and unclassified sequences. We then transformed genetic node heights into calendar times using the PoW distance-to-time transformation and obtained branch durations as differences between transformed parent and child node ages.

To propagate uncertainty, we sampled from the posterior distribution of short-term rates and from the posterior distribution of ultrametric distance trees. The resulting time-scaled trees were summarised as maximum clade credibility trees with median heights and assuming burn-in of 10% using TreeAnnotator. We used these reconstructions to estimate divergence times among major ANDV clades, to assess the deeper ancestry of the sampled ANDV lineage, and to compare the timescale of major reservoir-associated clades with the recent human outbreaks through which many lineages were detected.

Supplementary Table 1. Sequence metadata and inclusion status. Full metadata for all sequences used in the analysis, including accession, segment, host, country, collection date, source database, submitter or source study, clade assignment, inclusion/exclusion status and analysis subset.

Supplementary Table 2. Matched Accession IDs across all segments for the same sample/isolate.

Isolate name, country, host, collection date and accessions corresponding to each segment are provided. Supplementary Table 3. Sequences with uncertain collection dates and assigned sampling-date priors. Sequences lacking exact collection dates, inferred sampling intervals from source publications, and uniform priors used in molecular clock analyses.

Supplementary Table 4. BETS run effective sample size (ESS).

Log-likelihood values and Bayes factor (BF) reported for different sets of data comparing heterochronous (het) and isochronous (iso) models including/excluding starting tree (incl/excl). All datasets were run for 200M iterations with 20 steps, datasets indicated with an asterisk failed at 20 steps and were re-run with 10 steps. Datasets which have BF below 5 have been considered to show lack of evidence of temporal signal (see Methods) and have been indicated. Results are shown for the 'Observed' sequences under a strict clock, 'Observed' sequences under a relaxed clock, and 'All' (linkage-informed) sequences under a strict clock, annotated accordingly at the top row of each sub-table.

Supplementary Table 5. Inferred clock rate estimates.

Posterior mean, median and 95% highest posterior density intervals for substitution rate estimates across segments, clade compositions, and scenarios. Unless stated otherwise, estimates are inferred under a strict molecular clock model. All estimates are given as substitutions/site/year. Asterisks next to the dataset name indicate analyses for which BETS did not support the presence of a temporal signal. Supplementary Table 6. Sequences included in the two-per-outbreak sensitivity analyses. Accession IDs for the reduced "2pO" datasets, in which the two earliest available samples from each outbreak cluster were retained to assess the effect of dense sampling of near-identical outbreak genomes on molecular clock estimates.

Supplementary Table 7. Stem-branch mutation reconstruction.

Nucleotide and amino acid mutations within the coding regions inferred on branches leading to human outbreak-associated lineages, with synonymous/nonsynonymous classification, protein annotation. Genome nucleotide positions are with respect to reference for each segment-S: NC_003466.1,M: NC_003467.2 and L: NC_003468.2. Supplementary Table 8. Within-host variants in MV Hondius blood and nasal samples. Within-host single-nucleotide variants identified in the paired MV Hondius blood and nasal samples. Variants were included if they had a minimum iSNV frequency of 5% and were supported by at least two reads. Yellow highlighting indicates iSNV positions that were also reconstructed as mutations on one or more of the five outbreak stem branches. Reference genomes are S: NC_003466.1, M: NC_003467.2 and L: NC_003468.2. Sample identifiers are XDHK: PP_006XDHK.5 and XDJH: PP_006XDJH.5.
